title: The Autonomous Engine
subtitle: The Control Loops of the Human Body

chapters.title: The Hydraulic Impedance
chapters.subtitle: Otto Frank, Ernest Starling, and Myocardial Compliance in London
chapters.historical_anchor: Inside the physiology laboratory at University College London in the spring of 1914, Ernest Starling observed an isolated canine heart. The organ sat mounted within a scaffold of glass cannulae, brass pressure reservoirs, and mercury manometers.
chapters.exit_fact: That elastic expansion stores kinetic energy as wall tension and recoils during diastole to keep blood moving smoothly through peripheral tissue beds.

chapters.title: The Countercurrent Multiplexer
chapters.subtitle: Werner Kuhn and the Medullary Osmotic Gradient in Basel
chapters.historical_anchor: No biological membrane in the animal kingdom possesses a molecular pump capable of driving neutral water molecules uphill against an osmotic gradient. Yet human kidneys routinely excrete urine four times more concentrated than blood plasma.
chapters.exit_fact: That hormone inserts aquaporin-2 channels into the collecting duct wall so water diffuses passively into the $1,200\text{ mOsm/kg}$ medulla.

chapters.title: The Convective Sieve
chapters.subtitle: Christian Bohr, August Krogh, and Alveolar Gas Exchange in Copenhagen
chapters.historical_anchor: At the University of Copenhagen physiological laboratory in 1904, Danish physician Christian Bohr, assisted by Karl Hasselbalch and August Krogh, measured the oxygen-binding curves of whole blood inside custom tonometers. For decades, physiologists had assumed that hemoglobin bound oxygen like a simple bimolecular chemical reagent.
chapters.exit_fact: Without any neural command, local waste chemistry forces the protein to unload up to eighty percent of its oxygen cargo directly into the starving muscle fibers.

chapters.title: The Homeostatic Brake
chapters.subtitle: Walter Holbrook Gaskell and Parasympathetic Vagal Hysteresis in Cambridge
chapters.historical_anchor: Severed from all neural connections in an oxygenated surgical bath, or transplanted into a recipient's chest, the human heart beats at an intrinsic rhythm of 100 to 110 contractions per minute. Yet a healthy adult sitting quietly in a chair exhibits a resting pulse of 60 beats per minute.
chapters.exit_fact: By holding the resting heart under a fast-release tonic brake rather than relying on a slow accelerator, the circulation can double its output almost instantaneously simply by lifting vagal inhibition.

chapters.title: The Convective Flush
chapters.subtitle: Maiken Nedergaard and Glymphatic Interstitial Clearance in Rochester
chapters.historical_anchor: Fluorescent tracers injected into the cerebrospinal fluid of living mice in 2012 exposed a macroscopic clearance circuit inside the mammalian brain that anatomists had overlooked for more than a century. At the University of Rochester Medical Center, Danish neuroscientist Maiken Nedergaard and her colleague Jeffrey Iliff observed the living cerebral cortex through a two-photon laser scanning microscope.
chapters.exit_fact: Hydraulic resistance plummets, CSF rushes through the widened parenchyma, and amyloid-beta clearance accelerates twenty-fold.

chapters.title: The Calcium Trigger
chapters.subtitle: Setsuro Ebashi and the Troponin Molecular Switch in Tokyo
chapters.historical_anchor: When pure actin filaments and pure myosin filaments are extracted from rabbit skeletal muscle and mixed in a glass beaker with adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the proteins precipitate into an immediate, irreversible contraction. In 1942 at the University of Szeged, Albert Szent-Györgyi had demonstrated that extracted actomyosin threads contract violently upon contact with ATP.
chapters.exit_fact: Troponin I snaps tropomyosin back over the binding sites, and the muscle relaxes.

chapters.title: The Photonic Transducer
chapters.subtitle: George Wald and Retinal Rhodopsin Isomerization at Woods Hole
chapters.historical_anchor: A single photon of green light at a wavelength of 500 nanometers carries an energy quantum of roughly $2.48\text{ electron-volts}$, or $4 \times 10^{-19}\text{ Joules}$. That energy is fifteen orders of magnitude smaller than the kinetic energy of a falling snowflake.
chapters.exit_fact: Hundreds of membrane channels snap shut, blocking $10^7$ sodium ions from entering and hyperpolarizing the cell membrane to slow its synaptic glutamate release onto downstream bipolar neurons.

chapters.title: The Thermal Core
chapters.subtitle: Carl von Voit, Max Rubner, and Metabolic Energy Conservation in Munich
chapters.historical_anchor: Inside the Physiological Institute of the University of Munich in 1894, Max Rubner sealed a small experimental dog inside a double-walled copper chamber submerged in an insulated water bath. Trained under Carl von Voit, Rubner had spent a decade building the world's first high-precision animal respiration calorimeter to settle the central dispute of nineteenth-century biology.
chapters.exit_fact: Secreting up to 2 liters of hypotonic fluid per hour, evaporation sheds over 1,300 watts of thermal load through phase change.

chapters.title: The Electrochemical Gate
chapters.subtitle: Alan Hodgkin, Andrew Huxley, and the Axonal Voltage Clamp in Plymouth
chapters.historical_anchor: Measuring nearly one millimeter in diameter, the giant axon of the Atlantic squid (*Loligo forbesii*) is one hundred times thicker than a mammalian motor nerve fiber. In 1939, it was the only nerve fiber known to science large enough to let an experimenter thread a glass capillary electrode straight down its intracellular core without tearing the outer membrane.
chapters.exit_fact: That insulation forces the action potential to leap electrotonically between uninsulated nodes of Ranvier at velocities up to $120\text{ meters per second}$.

chapters.title: The Master Oscillator
chapters.subtitle: Colin Pittendrigh, Seymour Benzer, and Suprachiasmatic Phase Alignment in Pasadena
chapters.historical_anchor: Almost every biochemical reaction in a test tube obeys Svante Arrhenius's exponential rate law. Reaction velocity doubles or triples for every ten-degree Celsius rise in temperature ($Q_{10} = 2.0 \text{ to } 3.0$).
chapters.exit_fact: That glutamatergic pulse induces immediate *Per1* transcription and advances oscillator phase into exact lockstep with the rotation of the Earth.

chapters.title: The Acid-Base Servo
chapters.subtitle: John Scott Haldane, Lawrence Henderson, and the Medullary Chemoreceptor Loop in Oxford
chapters.historical_anchor: Arterial blood in a healthy human maintains a free hydrogen ion concentration ($[\text{H}^+]$) of roughly $40\text{ nanomoles per liter}$—one-millionth the concentration of blood sodium ions—corresponding to a pH of 7.40. Yet cellular metabolism pours roughly 15,000 millimoles of volatile carbonic acid and 70 millimoles of non-volatile sulfuric and phosphoric acids into the bloodstream every twenty-four hours.
chapters.exit_fact: That alkaline shift initially braked the medullary center until the kidneys excreted bicarbonate over four days to reset the $20:1$ buffer ratio at the new altitude.

chapters.title: The Glycemic Integral Controller
chapters.subtitle: Frederick Banting, Charles Best, and the Pancreatic Bihormonal Loop in Toronto
chapters.historical_anchor: At any moment, the entire five-liter blood volume of an adult human contains just four grams of dissolved free glucose. That single level teaspoon of sugar is held at a concentration near $90\text{ mg/dL}$ ($5.0\text{ mmol/L}$).
chapters.exit_fact: Within ninety minutes, arterial plasma glucose returns to its $90\text{ mg/dL}$ baseline with zero steady-state error.
